soak.e: From Middle English soken, from Old English socian (“to soak, steep”, literally “to cause to suck (up)”), from Proto-Germanic *sukōną (“to soak”), causative of Proto-Germanic *sūkaną (“to suck”).
soak.g: To be saturated with liquid by being immersed in it.

soap.e: From Middle English sope, sape, from Old English sāpe (“soap, salve”), from Proto-West Germanic *saipā, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb-, *seyp- (“to pour out, drip, trickle, strain”). Related also to Old English sāp (“amber, resin, pomade, unguent”), Latin sēbum (“tallow, fat, grease”).
soap.g: A metallic salt derived from a fatty acid, commonly used in cleaning products.

soap.e: Probably an abbreviation of sodium pentothal.

soar.e: From Middle English soren, from Old French essorer (“to fly up, soar”), from Vulgar Latin *exaurare (“to rise into the air”), from Latin ex (“out”) + aura (“the air, a breeze”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breath”).
soar.g: To fly high with little effort, like a bird.

sober.e: From Middle English sober, from Old French sobre, from Latin sōbrius, from se- (“without”) + ebrius (“intoxicated”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”).

soberly.e: From Middle English soberly; equivalent to sober + -ly.
soberly.g: In a sober manner; temperately; coolly; calmly; gravely; seriously.

soberness.e: From Middle English sobernes, sobrenesse; equivalent to sober + -ness.
soberness.g: The state or quality of being sober.

sobriety.e: From Old French sobriete, from Latin sobrietas.
sobriety.g: The quality or state of being sober.

socket.e: From Middle English socket, soket, from Anglo-Norman soket (“spearhead”), diminutive of Old French soc (“plowshare”), from Vulgar Latin *soccus, a word borrowed from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *sukkos (compare modern Welsh swch (“plowshare”)), literally "pig's snout", from Proto-Indo-European *suH-.
socket.g: Any of various concave objects (or portions of larger objects) that envelop a counterpart object.

sod.e: From the Old English plural past tense, or a back-formation from the past participle sodden.

sodden.e: From Middle English sodden, soden, from Old English soden, ġesoden, from Proto-Germanic *sudanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *seuþaną (“to seethe; boil”).
sodden.g: Soaked or drenched with liquid; soggy, saturated.

sodomite.e: From Middle English sodomyte, sodomite, from Old French Sodomite and Latin sodomīta, from Ancient Greek σοδομίτης (sodomítēs). Equivalent to Sodom + -ite.
sodomite.g: One who practices sodomy; a sodomist.

soever.g: In any fashion, of any kind; used for emphasis after words such as how, what, which etc.

soft.e: From Middle English softe, from Old English sōfte, alteration of earlier sēfte (“soft”), from Proto-West Germanic *samft(ī) (“level, even, smooth, soft, gentle”) (compare *sōmiz (“agreeable, fitting”)), from Proto-Indo-European *semptio-, *semtio-, from *sem- (“one, whole”).
From Middle English softe, from Old English sōfte (“softly”), from Proto-West Germanic *samftō (“softly”).
soft.g: Softly; without roughness or harshness; gently; quietly.

soften.e: From Middle English softenen, softnen, equivalent to soft + -en.
soften.g: To make something soft or softer.

softly.e: From Middle English softely, softeliche, equivalent to soft + -ly.

soil.e: From Middle English soile, soyle, sule (“ground, earth”), partly from Anglo-Norman soyl (“bottom, ground, pavement”), from Latin solium (“seat, chair; throne”), mistaken for Latin solum (“ground, foundation, earth, sole of the foot”); and partly from Old English sol (“mud, mire, wet sand”), from Proto-Germanic *sulą (“mud, spot”).
soil.g: A mixture of mineral particles and organic material, used to support plant growth.

soil.e: From Middle English soilen, soulen, suylen (“to sully, make dirty”), partly from Old French soillier, souillier (“to soil, make dirty, wallow in mire”), from Old Frankish *saulijan, *sulwijan (“to make dirty, soil”); partly from Old English solian, sylian (“to soil, make dirty”).

sojourn.e: From Middle English sojourne (noun) and sojournen (verb), from Old French sojor, sojorner (modern séjour, séjourner), from (assumed) Vulgar Latin *subdiurnāre, from Latin sub- (“under, a little over”) + Late Latin diurnus (“lasting for a day”), from Latin dies (“day”).

sojourner.e: From Middle English sogorner, sojorner, sugyner, equivalent to sojourn + -er.
sojourner.g: A person who resides temporarily in a place.

solace.e: From Old French solas, from Latin sōlācium (“consolation”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”).
solace.g: Comfort or consolation in a time of loneliness or distress.

sold.e: From Middle English solde, sould, soud, from Middle French solde, Italian soldo.

soldier.e: From Middle English soudeour, from Old French soudier or soudeour (“mercenary”), from Medieval Latin soldarius (“soldier (one having pay)”), from Late Latin solidus, a type of coin.
soldier.g: A member of a ground-based army, of any rank, but especially an enlisted member.

sole.e: From Middle English sole, soule, from Old French sol, soul (“alone”), from Latin sōlus (“alone, single, solitary, lonely”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (reflexive pronoun). Perhaps related to Old Latin sollus (“whole, complete”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“safe, healthy”).

From Middle English sole, soole, from Old English sole, solu. Reinforced by Anglo-Norman sole, Old French sole, from Vulgar Latin *sola (“bottom of the shoe”, also “flatfish”), from Latin solea (“sandal, bottom of the shoe”), from Proto-Indo-European *swol- (“sole”).
sole.g: The bottom or plantar surface of the foot.

solemn.e: From Middle English solempne, solemne (“performed with religious ceremony or reverence; devoted to religious observances, sacred; ceremonious, formal; of a vow: made under a religious sanction, binding; religious celebration, celebration of a feast day; famous, well-known; important; grand, imposing; awe-inspiring, impressive; grave, serious; dignified.
solemn.g: Of or pertaining to religious ceremonies and rites; (generally) religious in nature; sacred.

solemnity.e: From solemn + -ity, from Middle English solemnity (“observance of formality and ceremony”), frequently in the phrases in solemnity, with solemnity, which from Old French solemnite, from Latin sollemnitās, from sollemnis. (Compare solemn.)
solemnity.g: The quality of being deeply serious and sober or solemn.

solicit.e: From Middle English soliciten, solliciten, from Old French soliciter, solliciter, borrowed from Latin sollicitō (“stir, disturb; look after”), from sollicitus (“agitated, anxious, punctilious”, literally “thoroughly moved”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + perfect passive participle of cieō (“shake, excite, cite, to put in motion”).
solicit.g: To persistently endeavor to obtain an object, or bring about an event.

solid.e: From Middle English solide, borrowed from Old French solide, from Latin solidus (“solid”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂-i-dʰ-o-s (“entire”), suffixed form of root *solh₂- (“integrate, whole”).
solid.g: That can be picked up or held, having a texture, and usually firm. Unlike a liquid, gas or plasma.

solid.e: From Middle English solid, from the adjective, Middle French solide, or Latin solidum.
solid.g: A substance in the fundamental state of matter that retains its size and shape without need of a container (as opposed to a liquid or gas).

solitary.e: From Middle English solitarie, borrowed from Latin sōlitārius.
solitary.g: One who lives alone, or in solitude; an anchorite, hermit or recluse.

solve.e: From Middle English solven, from Latin solvō.
solve.g: To find an answer or solution to a problem or question; to work out.

some.e: From Middle English som, sum, from Old English sum (“some, a certain one”), from Proto-West Germanic *sum, from Proto-Germanic *sumaz (“some, a certain one”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one, whole”).
some.g: A certain number (multiple but not all).

somebody.e: From Middle English sum body, equivalent to some + body.

someone.e: From Middle English sum on, sum one, sum oon, equivalent to some + one.
someone.g: One or some person of unspecified or indefinite identity.

something.e: From Middle English somþyng, some-thing, som thing, sum thinge, sum þinge, from Old English sum þing (literally “some thing”), equivalent to some + thing.
something.g: An uncertain or unspecified thing; one thing.

sometime.e: From Middle English somtyme, som time, some tyme, sume time, sumtym, sumtyme, equivalent to some + time.
sometime.g: At an indefinite but stated time in the past or future.

sometimes.e: From Middle English sumtymes, somtymes, som tymes, equivalent to sometime + -s (adverbial suffix).
sometimes.g: On some occasions, over some periods, or in certain circumstances, but not always.

somewhat.g: To a limited extent or degree; not completely.

somewhere.g: In an uncertain or unspecified location.

son.e: From Middle English sonn, sone, sun, sune, from Old English sunu (“son”), from Proto-West Germanic *sunu, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *sewH- (“to bear; give birth”).
From Middle English sonen, sunen, from the noun (see above).
son.g: To produce (i.e. bear, father, beget) a son.

son-in-law.e: From Middle English sone in lawe; equivalent to son + -in-law.

song.e: From Middle English song, sang, from Old English sang, from Proto-West Germanic *sangu, from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz (“singing, song”), from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ- (“to sing”).
song.g: A musical composition with lyrics for voice or voices, performed by singing.

soon.e: From Middle English sone, from Old English sōna (“immediately, at once”), from Proto-West Germanic *sān(ō), from Proto-Germanic *sēna, *sēnô (“immediately, soon, then”), from *sa (demonstrative pronoun), from Proto-Indo-European *só (demonstrative pronoun).
soon.g: Short in length of time from the present.

soot.e: From Middle English soot, soote, sote, sot, from Old English sōt, from Proto-Germanic *sōtą (“soot”), from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”).
soot.g: Fine black or dull brown particles of amorphous carbon and tar, produced by the incomplete combustion of coal, oil etc.

sooth.e: From Middle English sooth, from Old English sōþ (“truth; true, actual, real”), from Proto-West Germanic *sanþ, from Proto-Germanic *sanþaz (“truth; true”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sónts, *h₁s-ont- (“being, existence, real, true”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”).

soothe.e: From Middle English sothen (“to verify, prove the validity of”), from Old English sōþian (“to verify, prove, confirm, bear witness to”), from Proto-West Germanic *sanþōn, from Proto-Germanic *sanþōną (“to prove, certify, acknowledge, testify”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”).
soothe.g: To restore to ease, comfort, or tranquility; relieve; calm; quiet; refresh.

soothsayer.e: From Middle English sothsaier, zothziggere, by surface analysis, sooth (“truth”) + sayer.
soothsayer.g: One who attempts to predict the future, using magic, intuition or intelligence; a diviner.

sop.e: From Middle English sop, soppe, sope, from Old English sopa (“sopped bread”), from Proto-Germanic *supô (compare Dutch sop, Old High German sopfa), deverbative of *sūpaną (“to sup”).

sorcerer.e: From Middle English sorcerere, from stem sorcer- (as in sorceresse and sorcery) + -ere, from Old French sorcer, sorcier, from Early Medieval Latin sortiārius, derived from Latin sortem (“fate, fortune”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”).
sorcerer.g: A magician or wizard. Sometimes specifically male.

sorceress.e: From Middle English sorceresse, from Anglo-Norman sorceresse.
sorceress.g: A female sorcerer, especially one who is elegant; compare witch.

sorcery.e: From Middle English sorcery, borrowed from Middle French sorcerie, ultimately derived from Latin sors (“fate”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”).
sorcery.g: Magical power; the use of witchcraft or magic arts.

sore.e: From Middle English sor, from Old English sār (“ache, wound”, noun) and sār (“painful, grievous”, adjective), from Proto-West Germanic *sair, from Proto-Germanic *sairaz (adjective) from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂iro-, enlargement of *seh₂y- (“to be fierce, afflict”).
sore.g: Causing pain or discomfort; painfully sensitive.

sore.e: From Middle English sor (“sorrel”), from Old French sor (“sorrel; reddish”).
sore.g: A young hawk or falcon in its first year.

sorely.e: From Middle English sorely, from Old English sārlīċ (adjective), sārlīċe (adverb); equivalent to sore + -ly.
sorely.g: In a sore or desperate manner.

sorrel.e: From Middle English sorel, from Old French sorel, surele (“sorrel”), from Old French sur (“sour”), of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sūraz (“sour”); equivalent to sour + -el (diminutive suffix).
sorrel.g: Any member of species of the genus Rumex of various plants with acidic leaves, especially

sorrel.e: From Middle English *sorel, from Middle French *sorel, sorrel, surrel, from Middle French sor (“yellowish-brown, reddish-brown”), probably from Old Frankish *sauʀ(ī) (“dried”), from Proto-Germanic *sauzaz (“dry”); equivalent to sore (“reddish-brown”) + -el (diminutive suffix).
sorrel.g: A brown colour, with a tint of red.

sorrow.e: From Middle English sorwe, sorow, sorewe, from Old English sorg, sorh (“care, anxiety, sorrow, grief”), from Proto-West Germanic *sorgu, from Proto-Germanic *surgō (compare West Frisian soarch, Dutch zorg, German Sorge, Danish, Swedish and Norwegian sorg), from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry.

sorroweth.g: third-person singular present simple form of sorrow

sorrowful.e: From Middle English sorweful, from Old English sorhful, sorgful (“full of care; anxious; sorrowful”), from Proto-Germanic *surgafullaz (“full of care; anxious”), equivalent to sorrow + -ful.
sorrowful.g: exhibiting sorrow; dejected; distraught; sad. (of a person)

sorry.e: From Middle English sory, from Old English sāriġ (“feeling or expressing grief, sorry, grieved, sorrowful, sad, mournful, bitter”), from Proto-West Germanic *sairag, from Proto-Germanic *sairagaz (“sad”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂yro (“hard, rough, painful”). By surface analysis, sor(e) + -y.
sorry.g: Of a person, regretful or apologetic for one's actions.

sort.e: From Middle English sort, soort, sorte (cognate Dutch soort, German Sorte, Danish sort, Swedish sort), borrowed from Old French sorte (“class, kind”), from Latin sortem, accusative form of sors (“lot, fate, share, rank, category”).
From Middle English sorten, from Old French sortir (“to allot, sort”), from Latin sortīre (“draw lots, divide, choose”), from sors.
sort.g: To separate items into different categories according to certain criteria that determine their sorts.

soul.e: From Middle English soule, sowle, saule, sawle, from Old English sāwol (“soul, life, spirit, being”), from Proto-West Germanic *saiwalu, from Proto-Germanic *saiwalō (“soul”), of an uncertain ultimate origin (. Scandinavian homonyms seem to have been borrowed from Old Saxon sēola.
soul.g: The spirit or essence of a person usually thought to consist of one's thoughts and personality, often believed to live on after the person's

sound.e: From Middle English sound, sund, isund, ȝesund, from Old English sund (“sound, safe, whole, uninjured, healthy, prosperous”), from Proto-West Germanic *sund, from Proto-Germanic *sundaz (“healthy”), merged with synonymous Old English ġesund, from Proto-West Germanic *gasund.

Noun: from Middle English sownde, alteration of soun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman sun, soun, Old French son, from accusative of Latin sonus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”). Verb: from Middle English sownden, sounen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman suner, sounder, Old French soner (modern sonner), from Latin sonō.
sound.g: A sensation perceived by the ear caused by the vibration of air or some other medium.

sounding.g: The action of the verb to sound.

soundly.e: From Middle English soundly, soundely, from Old English ġesundlīċe (“safely, prosperously, gladly”), equivalent to sound + -ly. Originally meaning "safely", the present sense came in the 16ᵗʰ century.
soundly.g: In a thorough manner; in manner free of defect or deficiency.

soundness.e: From Middle English soundenes, soundnes, from Old English *sundnes, *ġesundnes (attested in onsundnes), from Proto-West Germanic *sundnassī (“soundness, health”); equivalent to sound + -ness.
soundness.g: The state or quality of being sound.

sour.e: From Middle English sour, from Old English sūr (“sour”), from Proto-West Germanic *sūr, from Proto-Germanic *sūraz (“sour”), from Proto-Indo-European *súHros (“sour”).

source.e: From Middle English sours, from Old French sorse (“rise, beginning, spring, source”), from sors, past participle of sordre, sourdre, from Latin surgō (“to rise”), which is composed of sub- (“up from below”) + regō (“lead, rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti (“to straighten; right”), from the root *h₃reǵ-.
source.g: The person, place, or thing from which something (information, goods, etc.) comes or is acquired.

south.e: From Middle English south, from Old English sūþ, from Proto-West Germanic *sunþr (“southern”), from Proto-Germanic *sunþrą (“south”), from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”).
south.g: The direction towards the pole to the right-hand side of someone facing east, specifically 180°, or (on another celestial object) the direct

southeast.e: From Middle English southest, from Old English sūþēast, equivalent to south + east.
southeast.g: The intercardinal compass point halfway between east and south; specifically at a bearing of 135°.

southern.e: From Middle English southerne, sothern, sutherne, from Old English sūþerne (“southern, southerly, coming from the south; of southern make”), from Proto-Germanic *sunþrōnijaz (“southern”), from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂un-, *sh₂wen-, r/n-stem alternation of *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”). By surface analysis, south + -ern.
southern.g: Of, facing, situated in, or related to the south.

southwest.e: From Middle English southwest, southewest, from Old English sūþwest and sūþanwestan, equivalent to south + west.
southwest.g: The intercardinal compass point halfway between south and west; specifically at a bearing of 225°.

sovereign.e: From Middle English sovereyn, from Old French soverain (whence also modern French souverain), from Vulgar Latin *superānus (compare Italian sovrano, Spanish soberano) from Latin super (“above”). Spelling influenced by folk-etymology association with reign.

sovereignty.e: From Late Middle English sovereynte, souvereynte, from Anglo-Norman sovereyneté, soverentee, and Old French soveraineté, souveraineté (modern French souveraineté), from soverain + -té (suffix forming nouns, often denoting a property or quality). Soverain is derived from Vulgar Latin *superānus (“chief; sovereign”), from Latin super (“above.
sovereignty.g: The quality or state of being sovereign.

sow.e: From Middle English sowe, from Old English sugu, from Proto-West Germanic *sugu, from Proto-Germanic *sugō, probably from Proto-Indo-European *su(H)kéh₂, from *suH- (“pig”).
From Middle English sowen, from Old English sāwan, from Proto-West Germanic *sāan, from Proto-Germanic *sēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-.

sower.e: From Middle English sowere, from Old English sāwere; equivalent to sow + -er.
sower.g: One who or that which sows.

sown.g: Cultivated land inhabited by sedentary agriculturalists, in contrast to the nomad pastoralists of the steppe or desert.

seek.e: From Middle English seke, seken, from Old English sēċan, sēċean, sœ̄ċan, from Proto-West Germanic *sōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną (“to seek”), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂gyeti (“to seek out”), from *seh₂g- (“to follow, trace”). The Middle English and later Modern English hard /k/ derives from Old English sēcð, the third person singular.
seek.g: To try to find; to look for; to search for.
